content:
# Print Quality Control and Inspection Workflow

Quality control (QC) separates professional production from amateur work. Systematic inspection catches defects before shipping, prevents returns, and builds customer trust. This workflow covers color accuracy, registration, durability testing, and establishing defect standards.

## QC Stations and Equipment

**Visual Inspection Station**
- Bright, flicker-free LED lighting (5000K color temperature)
- Magnifying glass (5–10x magnification) for detail inspection
- Color reference swatch (Pantone or ICC profile target)
- Defect classification chart

**Color Measurement**
- Spectrophotometer (high-end) or colorimeter (budget option) for ∆E (color difference) measurement
- Measure printed garment against color standard
- ∆E < 2 = acceptable match; ∆E 2–5 = minor shift; ∆E > 5 = unacceptable

**Registration Accuracy Tools**
- Magnifying glass with crosshair reticle
- Ruler (0.1" precision) for measuring misalignment
- Acceptable tolerance: ±0.1" on most prints

**Durability Testing**
- Wash testing machine (AATCC or equivalent standard)
- Colorfastness reference cards (AATCC Blue Wool Scale)
- UV light box for light-fastness testing

## QC Inspection Checklist

**Before Production Starts (Setup QC)**
- [ ] Verify color matches customer swatch or reference (within ∆E < 2)
- [ ] Check registration alignment on first garment (measure misalignment)
- [ ] Inspect curing: no yellowing, stiffness, or ink beading
- [ ] Verify ink adhesion (pull test: ink should not flake or peel)
- [ ] Confirm garment size and fit on first sample

**During Production (Statistical Sampling)**
- [ ] Every 10th garment: full visual inspection
- [ ] Check color consistency across batch
- [ ] Monitor for ink buildup or curing drift
- [ ] Note any registration drift or misalignment patterns

**Final Inspection (Before Shipping)**
- [ ] Visual inspection: no visible defects, cracks, or ink pooling
- [ ] Color match: measure ∆E against standard
- [ ] Adhesion test: scratch ink lightly with fingernail; no flaking
- [ ] Stiffness check: flex garment; ink should move with fabric, not crack
- [ ] Package and label

## Defect Classification

**Critical Defects** (Reason for rejection)
- Missing color or registration > 0.2"
- Ink bleeding outside design boundaries > 1/8"
- Visible creasing or permanent damage to garment
- Ink peeling or flaking under normal handling
- Color ∆E > 5 from standard

**Major Defects** (Document, may reject if > 2 per batch)
- Registration off by 0.1–0.2"
- Color ∆E 2–5 from standard
- Minor ink pooling or texture irregularity
- Small yellowing or heat damage (< 1/4 inch)
- Ink stiffness noticeable but not cracking

**Minor Defects** (Accept if isolated, < 1 per 10 units)
- Registration off by < 0.1"
- Color ∆E 0.5–2 from standard
- Dust or lint embedded in ink
- Very slight yellowing
- Visible printing imperfection not affecting wearability

## Durability Testing Protocol

**Wash Test**
1. Print a test garment on the first day of production.
2. Launder 5 times in hot water (AATCC Standard Test Method 135).
3. Air dry (avoid dryer heat, which can set stains).
4. Inspect color change and fabric damage.
5. Grade using AATCC colorfastness scale (5 = no change, 1 = severe fading).
6. Document results; batch must meet minimum grade 3 for acceptance.

**Curing Adequacy Test**
1. Print test garment; immediately cure per spec.
2. Perform adhesion pull test: press masking tape firmly on ink, pull at 90° angle.
3. If any ink transfers to tape: under-cured. Increase dwell time or temperature.
4. Repeat test after adjustment; pass = no ink transfer.

**Scratch Resistance Test**
1. Use fingernail or plastic scraper to lightly scratch cured ink.
2. If ink cracks, flakes, or dulls: under-cured or wrong ink type.
3. If ink shows no damage: properly cured.

## Documentation and Trending

**Daily QC Log**
- Date, time, machine, operator
- Color ∆E readings (3–5 measurements per shift)
- Registration accuracy (average ∆ from standard)
- Defect count by category
- Corrective actions taken

**Weekly Trending**
- Plot color consistency across days and machines
- Identify patterns in defects (e.g., drift over time suggests curing station calibration issue)
- Calculate reject rate; target < 2% for high-quality shops

**Monthly Review**
- Review all defect data; identify top 3 root causes
- Schedule maintenance or retraining if needed
- Compare to customer complaints; adjust standards if mismatch detected

## Common QC Issues

**Color Drifts Throughout Shift**: Curing station temperature rising as it stabilizes. Allow longer warm-up time (20–30 minutes) and recalibrate every 4 hours.

**Registration Gradually Misaligns**: Machine drift, worn guides, or printer calibration shift. Check and recalibrate press or DTG position control.

**High Reject Rate (> 5%)**: Systematic issue (under-curing, poor pretreatment, wrong ink). Investigate root cause before continuing production.

**Inconsistent Color Between Machines**: Different ICC profiles or calibration on each machine. Standardize profiles and synchronize temperature settings.

content:
# High-Volume Batch Processing Workflow

Batch processing groups similar jobs for efficient setup and production. A well-organized batch workflow minimizes setup time, reduces waste, maximizes machine utilization, and improves profitability. This guide covers nesting strategies, setup procedures, scheduling, and measuring batch efficiency.

## Batch Planning

**Batch Criteria**
- **Same Garment Type**: All 11oz mugs, all medium t-shirts, etc. Different sizes = different setup time.
- **Similar Color**: Group light designs together, dark designs together. Changing curing temperature adds setup time.
- **Related Process**: All pretreatment, all DTG print, all heat-press cure. Don't mix process stages.
- **Common Tools**: All designs using same template or setup reduce retooling.

**Batch Sizing Strategy**
- **Small Batches** (5–10 units): For custom or rush orders. Setup time is significant fraction of total production time.
- **Medium Batches** (20–50 units): Most efficient for small shops (1–2 presses). Setup overhead amortized well.
- **Large Batches** (100+ units): Ideal for high-volume production. Setup time becomes negligible per unit.
- **Queue Optimization**: Plan 2–3 batches per day so setup time is only 15–20% of total.

## Pre-Production Setup

**1. Sort and Stage Work**
- Collect all garments for the batch; count and verify quantity.
- Arrange by color if possible (light → medium → dark).
- Lay out all design files on desktop; verify all are production-ready.
- Pre-heat press and curing station 20–30 minutes before start.

**2. Configure Machines**
- **For DTG**: Load garment size and pretreatment settings; test print on scrap garment.
- **For Screen Printing**: Mount screen; adjust squeegee pressure; flood pass to verify ink flow.
- **For Heat Press**: Set temperature, pressure, and dwell time; verify with test garment.
- **Document Settings**: Write down all parameters on production sheet for consistency.

**3. Prepare Materials**
- **DTG**: Load paper into pretreatment sprayer; fill ink reservoirs if running low.
- **Screen Printing**: Mix ink to correct viscosity; add to screen coating station.
- **Heat Press**: Lay out blank garments near press in sequential order.

## Production Sequencing

**Phase 1: Pretreatment** (if DTG)
1. Load first 10 garments into spray booth.
2. Spray evenly; send through conveyor dryer.
3. Stack treated garments on cart; keep warm.
4. Repeat until all garments treated.

**Phase 2: Printing**
1. Load first pretreated garment onto print bed.
2. Print design; verify print position and quality.
3. If acceptable, continue with remaining garments.
4. Queue printed garments for curing.

**Phase 3: Curing**
1. Transfer printed garments to heat press or curing conveyor immediately.
2. Cure per specification.
3. Remove and cool on rack.
4. Stack onto final pallet.

**Phase 4: Quality Check and Packaging**
1. Inspect every 10th garment; check color, registration, and adhesion.
2. Fold and bag completed garments.
3. Label with order number and date.
4. Stage for shipping.

## Efficiency Metrics

**Production Rate** = Total garments completed / Total time (including setup)
- Target: 10–20 units/hour for small shops; 30–50+ for industrial automation
- Track by batch to identify bottlenecks

**Setup Time %** = Setup time / (Setup + Production time) × 100
- Ideal: 15–20% for batches of 20+ units
- Above 30%: Batch too small or process too complex; combine with next batch

**Quality Rate** = Accepted units / Total units completed × 100
- Target: > 95%
- Below 95%: Investigate curing, pretreatment, or machine calibration issues

**Utilization Rate** = Productive time / Available shift time × 100
- Target: 70–80% (includes break time, setup, QC)
- Below 70%: Machine idle time or scheduling inefficiency

## Nesting and Waste Reduction

**For Print-and-Cut (Sublimation, UV DTF)**
- Arrange designs on film/paper to minimize waste
- Rotate small designs to fill gaps
- Target: < 10% waste per sheet

**For Screen Printing**
- Use half-screens for small designs
- Nest multiple small designs on one screen
- One-color designs on shared screens to save screen inventory

**For DTG on Garments**
- Position design 3–4 inches from collar and sleeves
- Consistent placement across batch for smooth operation

## Scheduling and Workload Balancing

**Daily Schedule Example** (3 batches, 8-hour shift)
- 7:00–7:30 AM: Setup; warm machines
- 7:30–9:00 AM: Batch 1 (30 units of design A)
- 9:00–9:30 AM: Setup Batch 2
- 9:30–11:00 AM: Batch 2 (25 units of design B)
- 11:00–11:15 AM: Lunch + Setup Batch 3
- 11:15–1:00 PM: Batch 3 (40 units of design C)
- 1:00–3:00 PM: QC and packaging; prep tomorrow's batches
- 3:00–5:00 PM: Shift end; cool and clean machines

**Capacity Planning**
- Identify your bottleneck (usually heat press or printer)
- Schedule batches to keep bottleneck machine busy 70–80% of shift
- Use secondary equipment (second heat press, second printer) to run parallel batches

## Common Batching Issues

**Inconsistent Results Between Batches**: Different operators, curing temperatures, or settings. Document all parameters; enforce consistency through checklists.

**Batch Larger Than Needed**: Order smaller batches to test before committing to full run. Reduces risk of high-volume defects.

**Too Many Setups**: Batch too small. Group with nearby batches or reschedule for higher efficiency.

**Machine Downtime During Batch**: Inadequate pre-production checks. Test print before loading full batch.

content:
# Print-and-Cut Registration and Contour Cutting Workflow

Print-and-cut combines DTG/screen printing with automated contour cutting for finished products (stickers, patches, decals). Accurate registration prevents misaligned cuts that ruin entire batches. This workflow covers design setup, registration marks, cutter calibration, and troubleshooting.

## Registration Systems

**Crop Mark Registration** (Most common)
- Printed crosshairs + corner marks define cut path
- Contour cutter scans marks and adjusts cut position accordingly
- Tolerates small film misalignment (typically ±1/8 inch)
- Ideal for print-and-cut applications

**Die-Cut Registration** (Precision cutting)
- Physical die (laser-cut metal) pressed onto printed substrate
- No marks needed; alignment via physical fit
- Best for high-precision, high-volume production
- Requires die manufacturing ($200–500+)

**Manual Registration** (Budget option)
- Operator manually positions substrate under cutter
- Works for small jobs but prone to human error
- Not recommended for batches > 5 units

## Design and File Preparation

**File Structure**
1. **Print Layer**: Full-color artwork (CMYK or RGB)
2. **Cut Layer** (Spot color): Defines contour path, printed as invisible registration marks or visible cut line
3. **Registration Marks**: Corner crosshairs (typically 0.2"×0.2" in contrasting color)
4. **Bleed**: 0.25" border around design for cutter tolerance

**Contour Layer Setup**
- Draw cut path 0.1–0.2 inches outside visible artwork
- Use a unique spot color (e.g., bright red) that doesn't appear in main artwork
- Ensure path is continuous with no breaks or overlaps
- Path width: 0.001–0.01 inches (thin line tells cutter to cut at center)

**Registration Mark Positioning**
- Place corner marks outside print area, 0.5 inches from edges
- Mark should be a simple crosshair: vertical and horizontal lines crossing at center
- Mark size: 0.2"×0.2" typical
- Ensure marks are on cut layer so cutter can detect them

## Print-and-Cut Workflow

**Phase 1: File Export**
1. Export design with all layers (print + cut layer) to PDF or TIFF
2. Verify registration marks are visible and properly positioned
3. Check that contour path is continuous and properly offset from artwork
4. Save two files: one for print (color channels), one for cut (spot color layer)

**Phase 2: Print to Carrier Film**
1. Load film into DTG or screen print press
2. Print color artwork + registration marks
3. Cure per specification
4. Cool slightly; do not handle excessively

**Phase 3: Cutter Setup and Calibration**
1. Load printed film into contour cutter
2. Open cut file (usually PDF or proprietary format)
3. Cutter scans for registration marks
4. If detected: automatic alignment applied; proceed to cut
5. If not detected: manual registration required (time-consuming)

**Phase 4: Test Cut**
1. Run first 1–2 pieces on scrap or low-value substrate
2. Inspect: contour should trace 0.1–0.2 inches outside artwork
3. If misaligned: adjust offset in cutter software and retest
4. Approve test before running full batch

**Phase 5: Production Cutting**
1. Queue remaining pieces
2. Monitor first 3–5 cuts for consistent quality
3. If deviation detected, pause and recalibrate
4. Collect finished pieces; trim excess film if needed

## Cutter Calibration and Offset

**Offset Adjustment**
- If cut is too far outward: reduce offset by 0.05–0.1 inches
- If cut is too far inward: increase offset by 0.05–0.1 inches
- Test after each adjustment with a single piece
- Document final offset for future jobs

**Blade Sharpness**
- Dull blade will skip or crush material instead of cutting cleanly
- Replace blade after 3–6 months of heavy use
- Test on scrap material; if resistance increases or tears occur, replace

**Pressure and Speed**
- Cutter pressure: Adjust until blade just cuts through carrier film without pressing into platen
- Too much: damages substrate; too little: incomplete cuts
- Speed: Slower = cleaner cuts but longer time. Faster = may compromise cut quality
- Start at medium speed; adjust based on results

## Common Issues and Fixes

**Registration Marks Not Detected**
- Marks too faint or misaligned. Reprint with higher ink coverage.
- Marks outside cutter's scanning area. Reposition marks 0.5 inches from edges.
- Mark color bleeding or distorted. Use pure spot color (no gradients).

**Contour Cuts Misaligned (Wavy or Off-Center)**
- Film shifted during print. Ensure film is flat on print bed; use tape if needed.
- Cutter calibration drift. Run calibration test again; adjust offset.
- Carrier film warped or stretched. Use fresh film stock.

**Incomplete Cuts (Partial or Skipped)**
- Blade too dull. Replace blade.
- Pressure too low. Increase cutter pressure by 1–2 levels.
- Speed too fast. Reduce cut speed by 10–20%.
- Material too thick. Verify film spec; some films require two passes.

**Artwork Damaged During Cutting**
- Offset too small (cutting into artwork). Increase offset by 0.1 inches.
- Blade pressure too high. Reduce pressure slightly and retest.
- Material too soft. Switch to more rigid film type.

## Production Tips

**Batch Consistency**: Run registration test on every 20th piece to ensure cutter hasn't drifted.

**Film Storage**: Keep film flat and dry. Humidity and heat can cause warping and registration issues.

**Quick Changeover**: Save cutter settings (offset, pressure, speed) for each design. Reloading is faster than recalibrating.

# Printing on Specialty Substrates Workflow

Printing extends beyond apparel to wood, acrylic, metal, glass, ceramics, and leather. Each substrate has unique surface properties, requires different inks and prep, and demands specific curing methods. Master substrate selection and production techniques to expand product offerings.

## Substrate Categories and Properties

**Porous Substrates** (Wood, Leather, Unglazed Ceramic)
- Absorb liquid inks quickly
- Require: Pre-treatment or sizing to control ink absorption
- Best inks: Water-based or dye-based (natural affinity for fiber)
- Curing: Air dry or low heat (if any)

**Non-Porous Substrates** (Metal, Glass, Glazed Ceramic, Plastic)
- Inks sit on surface; don't absorb
- Require: UV-curable inks or adhesion promoters
- Best inks: UV DTF, UV-curable plastisol, or specialized coatings
- Curing: UV light (20–45 seconds) or heat press (300–400°F)

**Semi-Porous Substrates** (Acrylic, Coated Wood, Laminate)
- Ink absorption varies by coating
- Require: Primers or adhesion sprays for maximum durability
- Best inks: Hybrid (UV + heat); UV DTF works best
- Curing: Combination UV + heat press for durability

**Flexible Substrates** (Leather, Textile Blends)
- Must flex without cracking or peeling
- Require: Flexible inks and proper underbase
- Best inks: Water-based screen print inks, flexible plastisol
- Curing: Low to medium heat; too high causes ink brittleness

## Substrate-Specific Preparation

**Wood**
- Sanding: 150–220 grit to open grain and improve adhesion
- Sizing: Apply wood sealer or inkjet pre-coat to prevent blotchy ink absorption
- Moisture: Acclimate wood 24–48 hours before printing (prevents warping after print)
- Best printing method: UV DTF or sublimation (if coated)

**Acrylic**
- Cleaning: Wipe with isopropyl alcohol to remove dust and oils
- Adhesion promoter: Optional but recommended for UV inks (improves durability)
- Coating: Check if surface is glossy or matte; glossy requires less prep
- Best printing method: UV DTF, UV-curable inks, or heat-transfer vinyl

**Metal**
- Cleaning: Remove grease with degreaser; light sandpaper roughens surface
- Primer: White metal requires primer or white base coat for color accuracy
- Oxidation: Bare aluminum oxidizes; use anodized or powder-coated metals when possible
- Best printing method: UV DTF (fastest), sublimation on coated metals

**Glass and Glazed Ceramic**
- Cleaning: Thorough degreasing and drying essential
- Surface texture: Smooth glass is challenging (poor ink adhesion). Frosted or textured surfaces work better.
- Primer: Not needed but adhesion spray improves durability
- Best printing method: UV DTF (cures instantly), specialty ceramic inks

**Leather**
- Testing: Always test on scrap leather first (vegetable-tanned vs. chrome-tanned absorb differently)
- Prep: Clean with leather cleaner; no sanding needed
- Inks: Water-based dyes or flexible screen print inks only (plastisol will crack on flex)
- Curing: Air dry or low heat (140°F max); high heat hardens leather

## Printing Method Selection by Substrate

**UV DTF (Best for Hard Surfaces)**
- Works on wood, acrylic, metal, glass, ceramic
- Cures in 20–45 seconds with UV light
- Excellent durability for outdoor applications
- Can apply immediately after cure (no cooling time)

**Sublimation (Best for Coated Surfaces)**
- Requires polyester or polymer coating (cannot use bare wood/metal)
- Dye bonds with coating molecules; highly durable
- No ink layer on surface (feels smooth)
- Heat press required: 350–400°F, 45–60 seconds

**Screen Printing (Traditional, Versatile)**
- Works on almost any surface (wood, metal, glass, ceramic)
- Requires manual or automated press
- Specialty inks available for each material
- Slower than UV DTF but often more cost-effective at high volume

**UV-Curable Plastisol (Hard Surface Alternative)**
- Similar to UV DTF but thicker ink layer
- Better coverage of surface texture and imperfections
- Requires UV curing after print
- More expensive than standard plastisol

## Production Workflow by Substrate

**Wood Printing (UV DTF Method)**
1. Sand wood (150–220 grit) to open grain
2. Wipe with damp cloth; air dry
3. Apply wood sealer or inkjet pre-coat if needed
4. Print design to UV DTF film
5. UV cure film (20–45 seconds)
6. Apply film to wood with heat press (350–375°F, 30–45 seconds) or transfer tape
7. Remove carrier film
8. Optional: topcoat with polyurethane for weather resistance

**Acrylic Printing (UV DTF or Heat Press)**
1. Clean with isopropyl alcohol; air dry
2. Print design to UV DTF film
3. UV cure (20–45 seconds)
4. Heat press to acrylic (375–400°F, 30–45 seconds)
5. Remove carrier film
6. Test adhesion; topcoat if necessary

**Metal Printing (UV DTF)**
1. Degrease metal with cleaner
2. Light sand (optional, improves adhesion)
3. Wipe clean
4. Print design to UV DTF film
5. UV cure (20–45 seconds)
6. Apply to metal via heat gun (350°F, 60 seconds) or heat press if flat
7. Let set 5 minutes; remove carrier film

**Leather Printing (Screen Print with Water-Based Ink)**
1. Clean leather with leather cleaner
2. Mount screen; adjust squeegee
3. Print design (water-based ink only—plastisol will crack)
4. Flash cure 20–30 seconds between layers if multi-color
5. Air dry or cure at 140°F for 2–3 minutes
6. Flex leather gently after curing to ensure ink flexibility

## Common Issues and Solutions

**Ink Not Adhering to Metal/Glass**: Surface oily or dusty. Degrease thoroughly and dry before printing.

**Ink Cracking on Leather**: Using plastisol or rigid ink. Switch to water-based or flexible plastisol; cure at lower temperature.

**UV Cure Too Fast (Bubbling)**: Film pulled out too early from curing station. Allow full exposure time.

**Dull or Washed-Out Colors on Wood**: Wood sealer over-applied. Use thinner coat; too much sealer blocks ink brilliance.

**Print Peeling After Heat Press**: Adhesion spray not used on smooth acrylic/metal. Reprint with primer or transfer tape.

faqs.question: Can I use regular DTG ink on non-fabric substrates?
faqs.answer: No. DTG inks are water-based and designed for fabric fibers. On hard surfaces, they won't cure or adhere. Use UV-curable inks or UV DTF for hard substrates.

faqs.question: What's the best way to prepare wood before printing?
faqs.answer: Sand with 150–220 grit to open the grain, wipe with damp cloth, air dry, and apply wood sealer or inkjet pre-coat to prevent blotchy absorption.

faqs.question: Can I print on bare aluminum or must it be anodized?
faqs.answer: Bare aluminum oxidizes quickly and has poor ink adhesion. Anodized aluminum is better. For bare aluminum, use a primer or white base coat first.

faqs.question: How do I print on textured or curved surfaces?
faqs.answer: Use transfer tape or adhesion spray (not heat press). Position design, press firmly by hand for 60 seconds, then slowly peel carrier film at 45° angle.

faqs.question: Can I use sublimation ink on wood?
faqs.answer: Only on pre-coated, polymer-sealed wood (which has polyester coating). Sublimation doesn't work on raw wood. Use UV DTF or water-based screen printing instead.
